name: Yugoslavia
sources: GDP ~$88bn and 23.5m people. Retail price inflation ran to roughly 580% over 1990, down from about 1250% in 1989, and output fell around 7%.

The game opens three weeks into Markovic's stabilisation programme (18 Dec 1989), which pegged the new dinar to the Deutschmark and froze wages, and the same month the League of Communists broke up at its 14th Congress, which is why separatism starts higher than the USSR's 0.55.

This block used to end "hence the punishing policy rate against still-enormous inflation", which the numbers beside it did not support and which has been removed. interest_rate 0.3 against inflation 0.6 is a real rate of -30 points: not punishing but the loosest opening position of any nation in the roster. Markovic's rate was genuinely punishing in real terms once the peg bit; the file was describing history the figures did not encode.

inflation 0.6 is not the 1990 print either. On this directory's fraction-of-1 convention ~580% is ~5.8; 0.6 is that shifted one decimal place — the same shift Brazil and Poland carry, and the same three nations whose 1990 percentage needed four digits. brazil.json records why the true figures cannot be entered as they stand: economy.rs clamps inflation into -0.05..=3.0 and the real-rate demand channel is linear and unbounded, so the corrected pair sends GDP through zero. The loader refuses figures outside that band since this commit.

Measured cost, so it is not rediscovered: on seed 1 Yugoslavia grows about 6% through 1990 — $88bn to $93.6bn — against a contraction of roughly 7%. Federal Yugoslavia comes apart on schedule anyway, because dissolution here is driven by the separatism arithmetic rather than by the growth path, but the economy it dies with is the wrong one.

pop_growth_1990 = 0.3980%/yr. The SFR Yugoslavia has no World Bank series of its own, so this is the SUM of the six republics' World Bank SP.POP.TOTL (SRB HRV BIH SVN MKD MNE): 21,325,807 in 1984 to 21,753,601 in 1989, compounded over the five years ending on the eve of the start date. DISCLOSED LIMIT: the World Bank's Serbia series excludes Kosovo, which had both the fastest population growth in the federation and about 1.9m people in 1990, so the sum reaches 21,753,601 against this file's transcribed population_m of 23.5 and this rate is a LOWER BOUND on the federation's. Kosovo has no World Bank series before 2008, so there is nothing to add that would not be invented.

note: 1990 TECHNOLOGY: AUTHORED, NOT DERIVED. What this nation knew on 1 January 1990 is transcribed and sourced grant by grant, exactly like every other 1990 figure in this file, and is not read off tfp_trend - there was never a code path from the trend to the known set, and the zero that stood there was a claim about the world rather than an absence of one (BIBLE section 8 and iron rule 4, both amended 2026-08-30). THE PREDICATE IS SPLIT, and split by the technology's OWN EFFECT TYPE so that it is mechanically computable and never a per-nation judgement call. A node whose effects include MilitaryEfficiency, MilitaryStrength, DiffusionEmission or CostReduction is SOVEREIGNTY-SIDE: holding it means this nation could PRODUCE it, so operating an imported article does not qualify. Every other node is USE-SIDE: deployed and in operational use here is enough, whoever built it, because the effect such a node pays is a productivity, health or output effect and that effect is real in the country where the machine runs. Of the 48 technologies the tree lets anyone hold in 1990, 17 are sovereignty-side and 31 are use-side.

ALL 48 OF THE 1990-ELIGIBLE TECHNOLOGIES WERE RULED FOR THIS NATION, one at a time, against a standard published per technology rather than per country. 2 were held and are listed below with their citations; 46 were refused. The refused ids are named at the end of this note so that a reader can tell a cell that was examined and refused from a cell nobody looked at - those are different claims and the schema would otherwise flatten them into the same silence.

granted.source: Zagreb was the first city in Yugoslavia to have a digital exchange: an AXE-10 installed in the Vrapce district in 1981. Tesla had signed a technical cooperation contract with Ericsson in 1977 for the production of the AXE10, AXB20 and ASB systems, and the partners built roughly a hundred AXE exchanges in the fixed network (Ericsson Nikola Tesla company history, ericsson.hr). Yugoslavia both operated and manufactured them - but this is the use-side node, so operation is what is graded.

WUENIC has no 1990 value for Yugoslavia. R1 applied to the earliest published successor-state values: Slovenia 1992: 98%; Serbia 1992: 84%; Croatia 1992: 83%; North Macedonia 1993: 90% — every constituent republic the series reaches is at or above the 80% threshold in its first covered year, measured during the war rather than before it. Bosnia and Herzegovina prints 58% in 1992, mid-siege, and is excluded as a wartime measurement. PROXY CELL — not a 1990 measurement, and the war contaminates it downward, which biases toward the grant being conservative.
